# SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression

Shaowei Zhang ^(†)^(†)thanks: Work done during internship at SenseTime

###### Abstract

Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) has become a fundamental
capability for large language models (LLMs) in human-centric
interaction. Beyond accurate recognition, recent studies highlight the
importance of coherent emotional expression, yet both abilities are
severely limited by the scarcity and static nature of high-quality
annotated data.In this work, we propose SELF-EMO, a self-evolution
framework grounded in a psychologically motivated hypothesis: the better
a model predicts others’ emotions, the better it can generate its own
emotionally consistent responses. Building on this insight, we
explicitly incorporate two auxiliary tasks—emotional understanding and
emotional expression—and formulate a role-based self-play paradigm in
which the model simultaneously acts as an emotion recognizer and a
dialogue responder. Through iterative interaction, the agents
continuously generate diverse conversational trajectories, forming a
scalable data generation process. To ensure training quality, we
construct a data flywheel mechanism: each self-play rollout produces
multiple candidate emotional predictions and responses, which are then
filtered via a smoothed IOU-based reward to select high-quality samples.
The selected samples are fed back into training, enabling continuous
self-improvement without external supervision. Based on this paradigm,
we further develop SELF-GRPO, a reinforcement learning algorithm that
stabilizes optimization under diverse emotional outputs by combining
multi-label alignment rewards with group-level consistency
signals.Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets (IEMOCAP,
MELD, and EmoryNLP) demonstrate that SELF-EMO achieves state-of-the-art
(SOTA) performance without relying on external retrieval or auxiliary
models. Under a unified training setting, our method improves average
accuracy by +6.33% on Qwen3-4B and +8.54% on Qwen3-8B, with consistent
gains across all benchmarks. These results validate the effectiveness of
the proposed self-evolution paradigm and highlight its strong
generalization ability.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in daily human
life—not merely as tools, but as conversational partners [OpenAI
(2024)](#bib.bib18); [Yang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib16); [Grattafiori et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib3); [Liu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib4). This shift makes
emotionally intelligent interaction a pressing research priority, with
Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) emerging as a core task for
building more anthropomorphic AI systems [Zhang et al.
(2019)](#bib.bib2).

![Refer to caption](2604.18003v1/intru.png)

Figure 1: Comparison of prior work and SELF-EMO, a multi-task
self-evolution framework that unifies emotion recognition, emotional
understanding, and emotion-consistent response generation within a
closed-loop self-play paradigm.

Despite recent progress, existing LLM-based ERC methods remain
fundamentally limited by their reliance on static external knowledge.
Approaches based on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or auxiliary
LLM supervision  [Lei et al. (2024)](#bib.bib36); [Li et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib40); [Xue et al. (2024)](#bib.bib39) improve
in-distribution performance, but introduce a strong dependency on fixed
datasets and additional models. As a result, these methods fail to
generalize across datasets, with performance dropping significantly
under cross-domain settings. More importantly, these limitations point
to a deeper bottleneck: the lack of a scalable training signal. Current
ERC pipelines rely on static annotated datasets, which cannot provide
the diverse and continuously evolving supervision required for iterative
optimization. This creates a fundamental tension between performance,
efficiency, and generalization, preventing models from achieving robust
emotional intelligence.

To address this challenge, we propose SELF-EMO, a self-play
reinforcement learning framework that transforms emotional understanding
into a scalable training signal. Our approach is grounded in a
psychologically motivated hypothesis that is theoretically justified and
empirically validated in this work: the better a model predicts others’
emotions, the better it can generate its own emotionally consistent
responses.Building on this insight, we extend the standard ERC
formulation by introducing two auxiliary tasks—emotional understanding
and emotional expression—forming a structured pipeline from recognition
to response generation. We organize these tasks into a role-based
self-play paradigm, where persona-conditioned agents act as both an
emotion recognizer and a dialogue responder. Through iterative
interaction, the model generates diverse conversational trajectories
with emotion predictions, self-emotional states, and responses.To enable
scalable self-improvement, we further construct a data flywheel
mechanism. In each self-play rollout, multiple candidate predictions and
responses are generated, evaluated via a smoothed IOU-based reward, and
high-quality samples are selected and fed back into training. This forms
a closed loop of generation $`\rightarrow`$ selection $`\rightarrow`$
reuse, allowing continuous refinement without external supervision.To
optimize this process under diverse emotional outputs, we introduce
SELF-GRPO, a multi-emotion reinforcement learning algorithm that
combines multi-label alignment rewards with group-level consistency
signals for more stable credit assignment. This design provides both
theoretical and empirical support for the proposed self-evolution
paradigm.Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  SELF-EMO Framework: We propose a multi-task self-evolution framework
  that unifies emotion recognition, emotional understanding, and
  emotion-consistent response generation within a role-based self-play
  paradigm, enabled by a generate–filter–reuse data flywheel for
  continuous self-improvement.
- •
  SELF-GRPO Algorithm: We develop a multi-emotion reinforcement learning
  algorithm that enhances credit assignment via core emotion set
  aggregation and group-level consistency modeling, improving stability
  under diverse predictions.
- •
  Empirical Performance and Generalization: Extensive experiments show
  that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance with strong
  cross-dataset generalization, yielding accuracy gains of +6.33% on
  Qwen3-4B and +8.54% on Qwen3-8B.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 ERC Methods

Prior work in the field of ERC has primarily concentrated on three
methodological paradigms: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [Lipton et
al. (2015)](#bib.bib13), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [Scarselli et al.
(2008)](#bib.bib12), and Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) [Koroteev
(2021)](#bib.bib11). In RNN-based studies, DialogueRNN [Majumder et al.
(2019)](#bib.bib25) and DialogueCRN [Hu et al. (2021a)](#bib.bib9) adopt
RNN architectures to track contextual information and the individual
states of speakers throughout the conversation. In GNN-based studies,
models capture relational information by constructing graph structures
among utterances and speakers. For example, DialogueGCN [Ghosal et al.
(2019)](#bib.bib27) treats utterances as graph nodes and builds edges
based on contextual information, while DAG-ERC [Shen et al.
(2021)](#bib.bib30) further incorporates speaker identity and utterance
position into the graph. In studies based on pre-trained language
models, BERT-ERC [Qin et al. (2023)](#bib.bib10) leverages models such
as BERT and improves performance by introducing a fine-grained emotion
classification module and a two-stage training strategy.

With the rise of LLMs, current research in the ERC field mostly uses
LLMs combined with retrieval-augmented methods to improve model
performance on the ERC task, among which InstructERC [Lei et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib36) is the first study to introduce these methods in
this field. Subsequently, BiosERC [Xue et al. (2024)](#bib.bib39)
further adds character traits to the input and adopts LoRA [Hu et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib6) training to efficiently fine-tune the model.
Furthermore, PRC-Emo [Li et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib40) proposes to
additionally include internal and external emotional descriptions of
speakers in the input and employs a curriculum learning strategy to
enhance model performance. However, these works introduce static
knowledge bases for retrieval and incorporate external knowledge
analysis, which also lead to problems of poor model generalization
ability and high inference resource consumption.

### 2.2 Self-Play for Self-Evolution

Due to the rise of LLM-based methods, an increasing number of works have
begun to focus on how to achieve a closed training loop solely through
data generated by the model itself under the constraint of limited
high-quality human-crafted data [Fang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1); [Zhang
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib38); [Yang et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib37), thereby
significantly reducing the cost of manual data creation. This approach
has yielded substantial benefits in multiple domains. For instance,
AbsoluteZero [Zhao et al. (2025)](#bib.bib17) was proposed in the code
generation domain, training the model itself as a user instruction
generator to obtain high-quality problems while simultaneously training
its ability to solve the generated problems. In the mathematical
reasoning domain, works such as SVS [Liang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib15)
and PromptCot [Yao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib14) have also demonstrated
that the model itself can serve as a high-quality problem generator,
producing problems of appropriate difficulty for the model to perform
reinforcement learning and improve problem-solving performance. However,
self-play works all need to address a fundamental issue: how to design a
logically rigorous operational paradigm for self-play to achieve a
closed training loop.

### 2.3 Psychological Connections of Emotion Tasks

At present, there have already been a large number of psychological
studies that have made detailed arguments and experiments on the
connection among the three tasks of emotion understanding and
recognition, self-emotion generation, and expression. Among them, the
theory of levels of emotional awareness  [Lane and Schwartz
(1987)](#bib.bib21) indicates that individuals must first recognize,
differentiate, and label emotions before they can conduct more complex
emotional reasoning and social emotion regulation  [Fonagy et al.
(2018)](#bib.bib22), and the differentiation of others’ emotions is the
core of explaining others’ behaviors and generating appropriate
responses. On the contrary, existing clinical evidence  [Taylor et al.
(1999)](#bib.bib20) shows that the lack of emotional differentiation
ability will directly impair empathy and expression. These studies all
indicate that emotion understanding and recognition is the premise of
self-emotion generation and expression. Moreover, studies  [van der
Schalk et al. (2015)](#bib.bib23) show that others’ emotions will
influence the observer’s emotions and behavioral decisions, and the
occurrence of this phenomenon can be summarized as that how one
understands others’ emotions will directly control self-emotion
generation and expression.

## 3 Methodology

![Refer to caption](2604.18003v1/self-grpo-v2_cropped.png)

Figure 2: The overall framework of SELF-EMO.During SELF-GRPO tuning, the
model explicitly optimizes the ERC task and implicitly optimizes the
other two. High-quality samples generated during training are retained
for subsequent training.

In this section, we detail the SELF-EMO training framework, which
extracts rich situational and personality information from existing
datasets and constructs a closed-loop evolution paradigm across three
key psychological tasks: Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC),
emotional understanding, and emotional expression. We first provide the
theoretical proof for SELF-EMO’s semi-supervised mechanism.
Subsequently, we describe the algorithmic process of SELF-EMO and the
SELF-GRPO reinforcement learning algorithm designed to support self-play
data generation.

### 3.1 Semi-supervised Multi-task Entropy Reduction

We introduce two unsupervised auxiliary tasks to support the ERC task
$`T_{o}`$: self-personality understanding ($`T_{s}`$) and self-emotion
expression ($`T_{r}`$). Given a dialogue context $`C`$ and a personality
trait $`PI`$, the model produces three outputs sequentially:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
T_{o}=\pi_{\theta}(e_{o}\mid C,PI),\quad T_{s}=\pi_{\theta}(e_{s}\mid C,PI,e_{o}),\quad T_{r}=\pi_{\theta}(r\mid C,PI,e_{o},e_{s})
``` |  | (1) |

where $`e_{o}`$ is the predicted emotion of the interlocutor, $`e_{s}`$
is the model’s self-perceived emotional response, and $`r`$ is the
self-emotion expression generated by $`T_{r}`$.

##### Theoretical Derivation

Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, an agent’s internal state is
shaped by its appraisal of others’ emotions. We model this as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
T_{s}=f_{s}(T_{o},C,PI)+\epsilon_{s},\qquad T_{r}=f_{r}(T_{o},T_{s},C,PI)+\epsilon_{r}
``` |  | (2) |

where $`f_{s}`$ and $`f_{r}`$ are the appraisal and expression mappings,
and $`\epsilon_{s}`$, $`\epsilon_{r}`$ are residual terms.

From an information-theoretic perspective [Gao et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib24), optimizing $`T_{o}`$ via reinforcement learning
reduces the output entropy $`H_{\pi_{\theta}}(e_{o}\mid C,PI)`$. Given
the functional dependencies above, this propagates to the auxiliary
tasks:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\downarrow H_{\pi_{\theta}}(e_{o}\mid C,PI)\;\Rightarrow\;\downarrow H_{\pi_{\theta}}(e_{s}\mid C,PI,e_{o})\;\Rightarrow\;\downarrow H_{\pi_{\theta}}(r\mid C,PI,e_{o},e_{s})
``` |  | (3) |

This shows that supervised training on $`T_{o}`$ implicitly reduces
uncertainty in $`T_{s}`$ and $`T_{r}`$, providing a theoretical basis
for the unsupervised components in SELF-EMO.

### 3.2 Extracting Personality Information and Constructing Dialogue Data

Let
$`\mathcal{D}=\{\mathcal{D}_{\text{IEMOCAP}},\mathcal{D}_{\text{MELD}},\mathcal{D}_{\text{EmoryNLP}}\}`$
be the collection of source datasets, and let $`d\in\mathcal{D}`$ denote
a sampled dialogue segment. We use a large language model $`M_{e}`$,
guided by prompt $`P_{\text{extrac}}`$, to extract speaker personality
information $`PI`$ from each segment:

|     |                                |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       PI=M_{e}(d,P_{\text{extrac}}).
       ```                             |     | (4) |

To improve coverage and diversity, $`M_{e}`$ is instantiated with two
models: Seed-1.8, DeepSeek-V3.2.

Given historical context $`\mathit{C}`$ and personality information
$`PI`$, a generation model $`\pi_{\theta}`$ produces a structured
dialogue sample $`R^{\text{syn}}`$ through three sequential steps:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R^{\text{syn}}=\left[\underbrace{e_{o}=\pi_{\theta}(\mathit{C},\,PI)}_{\text{Others' Emotion Recognition}},\;\underbrace{e_{s}=\pi_{\theta}(\mathit{C},\,PI,\,e_{o})}_{\text{Self-Emotion Generation}},\;\underbrace{r=\pi_{\theta}(\mathit{C},\,PI,\,e_{o},\,e_{s})}_{\text{Self-Emotion Expression}}\right],
``` |  | (5) |

where $`e_{\text{o}}`$ is the recognized emotion of the interlocutor and
$`e_{\text{s}}`$ is the speaker’s generated self-emotion, and $`r`$ is
the final response. Since the three steps produce non-overlapping
outputs, $`\pi_{\theta}`$ generates all content in a single pass under
prompt $`P_{\text{gen}}`$. The resulting samples $`R^{\text{syn}}`$
serve as initialization data for the self-play training stage. All
prompts used above can be found in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Prompts ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression").

### 3.3 Data Closed-loop Self-play Reinforcement Learning Fine-tuning

During online sampling, for each input $`(PI,C_{ori})`$, the model
produces:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle(e_{o},e_{s},r,Output_{Dict})`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\theta}(e_{o},e_{s},r\mid C_{ori},PI)`$ |  | (6) |
|  | $`\displaystyle Prediction_{o},\,Label_{s},\,r`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim Extract(Output_{Dict})`$ |  |  |

where $`e_{o}`$ contains the emotion prediction $`Prediction_{o}`$ for
the last speaker, $`e_{s}`$ contains the model’s self-emotion label
$`Label_{s}`$ under the given personality, and $`r`$ is the generated
response. High-quality samples are used to construct new training data:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{new}\leftarrow C_{ori}\cup r,\quad Label_{new}\leftarrow Label_{s}
``` |  | (7) |

To handle the discrete ERC label space, we propose a multi-label
weighted reward. The model outputs up to $`N\!\leq\!3`$ emotion
predictions, each with a weight $`Weight^{emo_{n}}`$, yielding a
smoothed IOU-based reward:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle Prediction_{o}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{(Prediction^{emo_{n}},Weight^{emo_{n}})\}_{n=1}^{N}`$ |  | (8) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\cdot)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0,&rule(Output_{Dict})=0\\
IOU(Prediction_{o},\,Label_{ori|new})+0.1,&rule(Output_{Dict})=1\end{cases}`$ |  |  |

Let $`P=\{(e,\,w^{P}_{e})\}`$ and $`L=\{(e,\,w^{L}_{e})\}`$ denote the
raw prediction and label weight sets. We normalize each to sum to 1:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{w}^{P}_{e}=\frac{w^{P}_{e}}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}w^{P}_{e^{\prime}}},\quad\hat{w}^{L}_{e}=\frac{w^{L}_{e}}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}w^{L}_{e^{\prime}}}
``` |  | (9) |

Setting $`\hat{w}^{P}_{e}=0`$ for $`e\notin P`$ and
$`\hat{w}^{L}_{e}=0`$ for $`e\notin L`$, the weighted IOU is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{IOU}(P,L)=\frac{\sum_{e\in P\cup L}\min(\hat{w}^{P}_{e},\,\hat{w}^{L}_{e})}{\sum_{e\in P\cup L}\max(\hat{w}^{P}_{e},\,\hat{w}^{L}_{e})}
``` |  | (10) |

This gives partial credit for near-correct predictions.

##### SELF-GRPO

We extend GRPO [Shao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib19) into SELF-GRPO, which
introduces a secondary reward to improve consistency and stability
across rollouts within the same sampling group. For each rollout
$`y_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot|x)`$, the primary reward is
$`r_{i}=\mathcal{R}(y_{i})`$. We aggregate emotion distributions over
all $`n`$ rollouts to form a core distribution $`p^{*}`$ over the top-3
emotions $`\mathcal{E}_{\text{top3}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{p}(e)=\frac{\sum_{i}p_{i}(e)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\sum_{i}p_{i}(e^{\prime})},\quad p^{*}(e)=\frac{\tilde{p}(e)}{\sum_{e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{top3}}}\tilde{p}(e^{\prime})}
``` |  | (11) |

The secondary reward counts how many of the top-3 consensus emotions
appear in rollout $`y_{i}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{i}^{(2)}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{e\,\in\,\mathcal{E}_{\text{top3}}}\mathbf{1}[e\in Prediction_{i}]
``` |  | (12) |

Both rewards are normalized. The combination weight $`\lambda`$
increases linearly with training progress to encourage early exploration
and late consistency:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\lambda=\frac{t}{T},\quad A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\mu_{r}}{\sigma_{r}}+\lambda\,\frac{r_{i}^{(2)}-\mu_{r^{(2)}}}{\sigma_{r^{(2)}}}
``` |  | (13) |

where $`t`$ is the current step and $`T`$ is the total training steps.
The policy is updated by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{self\_grpo}(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min\!\left(\rho_{i}A_{i},\ \operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i},\,1{-}\epsilon,\,1{+}\epsilon)\,A_{i}\right),\quad\rho_{i}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_{i}\mid x)}
``` |  | (14) |

### 3.4 SELF-EMO Training Algorithm

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.4 SELF-EMO Training Algorithm ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression")
summarizes the full SELF-EMO training process. The framework starts from
a cold-start SFT stage, then alternates between two steps: SELF-GRPO
updates the policy on the current buffer $`\mathcal{B}`$, and the best
rollout per prompt is filtered back into $`\mathcal{B}`$ to retrain the
base model. Each iteration feeds better data into the next, forming a
self-improving closed loop.

1: Original dataset $`\mathcal{D}_{0}`$; replay buffer
$`\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{D}_{0}`$; reward $`\mathcal{R}(\cdot)`$;
iterations $`K`$; rollouts per prompt $`n`$

2: Optimized policy $`\pi_{\theta^{*}}`$

3: Cold Start: train $`\pi_{\theta}`$ on $`\mathcal{D}_{0}`$ via
supervised fine-tuning

4: for $`k=1`$ to $`K`$ do

5:   // RL stage: rollout and policy update

6:   for each prompt $`x`$ sampled from $`\mathcal{B}`$ do

7:    Sample $`n`$ rollouts
$`\{y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$

8:    Compute per-rollout rewards $`r_{i}=\mathcal{R}(y_{i})`$
(Eq. [8](#S3.E8 "In 3.3 Data Closed-loop Self-play Reinforcement Learning Fine-tuning ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"))

9:    Update policy:
$`\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\,\nabla_{\theta}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{SELF-GRPO}}`$
(Eq. [14](#S3.E14 "In SELF-GRPO ‣ 3.3 Data Closed-loop Self-play Reinforcement Learning Fine-tuning ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"))

10:   end for

11:   // Data selection: best rollout per prompt into buffer

12:   for each prompt $`x`$ do

13:    $`y^{*}=\arg\max_{i}\;r_{i}`$

14:    Construct $`d^{*}=(C_{new},Label_{new})`$ from $`y^{*}`$
(Eq. [7](#S3.E7 "In 3.3 Data Closed-loop Self-play Reinforcement Learning Fine-tuning ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"))

15:    $`\mathcal{B}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}\cup\{d^{*}\}`$

16:   end for

17:   // Closed-loop retraining on updated buffer

18:   Retrain base model $`\pi_{\theta}`$ on $`\mathcal{B}`$ via
supervised fine-tuning

19: end for

20: return $`\pi_{\theta}`$

Algorithm 1 SELF-EMO Closed-Loop Optimization

This design removes the need for manual data collection. By leveraging
ERC-related auxiliary tasks, the model generates and filters its own
training data throughout the process, keeping annotation costs low while
maintaining data quality via the reward-based selection in
Eq. [8](#S3.E8 "In 3.3 Data Closed-loop Self-play Reinforcement Learning Fine-tuning ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression").

## 4 Experiments

This section introduces the experimental setup, the experimental
results, and an analysis of the results.

### 4.1 Experimental Setting

Datasets. Our methodology is grounded in three widely recognized
benchmarks in the ERC domain: IEMOCAP  [Busso et al. (2008)](#bib.bib7),
MELD  [Poria et al. (2019)](#bib.bib8), and EmoryNLP  [Zahiri and Choi
(2018)](#bib.bib5). These datasets serve as the seed data for persona
initialization. Specifically, IEMOCAP consists of dyadic conversations
among ten speakers (5,163/647/1,623 samples for train/dev/test). MELD
and EmoryNLP, both derived from television series with multi-party
dialogue settings, comprise 9,989/1,109/2,610 and 7,551/954/984
utterances, respectively. All model evaluations are strictly performed
on the official test splits of these benchmarks.

Baselines. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, we compare it
against prominent ERC methods, categorized into two groups: (1)
Traditional methods, including DialogueRNN  [Majumder et al.
(2019)](#bib.bib25), ICON  [Hazarika et al. (2018)](#bib.bib26),
DialogueGCN  [Ghosal et al. (2019)](#bib.bib27), COSMIC  [Ghosal et al.
(2020)](#bib.bib28), MMGCN  [Hu et al. (2021b)](#bib.bib29), DAG-ERC
 [Shen et al. (2021)](#bib.bib30), LR-GCN  [Ren et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib31), Multi-DAG+CL  [Nguyen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib32),
CBERL  [Meng et al. (2023)](#bib.bib33), DER-GCN  [Ai et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib34), and LSDGNN+ICL [Li et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib35); (2)
LLM-based methods, such as InstructERC  [Lei et al. (2024)](#bib.bib36),
BiosERC  [Xue et al. (2024)](#bib.bib39), and PRC-EMO  [Li et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib40).

Implementation Details. The experiments are conducted on a cluster of
eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs, utilizing Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B  [Yang et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib16) as the primary backbone models. Departing from the
common practice where models are restricted to single-dataset training—a
setup prone to overfitting and limited generalization—this work adopts a
more robust strategy. Specifically, a single unified model is trained
across all three ERC training sets and subsequently evaluated on each
official test split. For a rigorous and fair comparison, the two most
competitive LLM-based baselines are retrained under this identical
multi-dataset setting. Additional hyperparameter configurations and
training details are provided in Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Hyperparameter Configuration ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression").

### 4.2 Main results

As shown in Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
under the unified training setting, existing LLM-based methods exhibit
limited generalization across different conversation contexts. In
contrast, the proposed SELF-EMO framework achieves substantial
performance gains. Specifically, our model realizes an accuracy increase
of +6.33% on the Qwen3-4B backbone and +8.54% on the Qwen3-8B backbone,
with consistent improvements observed across all benchmarks. These
results demonstrate the robust generalization of SELF-EMO and
empirically validate the effectiveness of the self-evolution paradigm in
enhancing emotional intelligence through autonomous agent interactions.

### 4.3 Ablation Experiments

We conduct ablation experiments on SELF-EMO-4B to assess each
component’s contribution (Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Experiments ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression")).
Regarding the data produced by SELF-EMO, w/ COLD uses the cold-start
data generated by the expert model to first perform SFT, and then uses
the resulting model as the base model for the RL training stage. w/o
SELF-GRPO indicates that we directly apply the vanilla GRPO algorithm
for RL-stage fine-tuning. w/o SELF-EMO indicates that we train with GRPO
using all data from the original datasets.

[TABLE]

Table 2: Ablation experiments on each component.

The experiments demonstrate that our method does not rely on data
produced by the expert model. Instead, during the cold-start phase, the
model only learns the corresponding reasoning and output patterns, and
incorporating expert-generated data for SFT actually degrades model
performance. SELF-GRPO enables the model to perform macro-level reward
modeling over sampled outputs, leading to more stable emotional
understanding outputs and consequently improved performance. Overall,
both the self-play data generated by SELF-EMO and the training algorithm
are crucial to the model’s performance gains; applying GRPO fine-tuning
with only the original data leads to a sharp average performance drop of
5.18%.

### 4.4 Analysis

![Refer to caption](2604.18003v1/picture/cot_comparison.png)

(a) Self-personality understanding

![Refer to caption](2604.18003v1/picture/response_comparison.png)

(b) Self-emotion expression

Figure 3: Performance improvement on two self-supervised tasks. DeepSeek
and Seed serve as judges for A/B testing on generated responses.
SELF-EMO significantly boosts response quality after training.

#### 4.4.1 Performance Improvement on Self-supervised Tasks

As shown in
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
we collect online sampled examples from models at the early stage of RL
training and the later stage of training, and randomly sample them for
analysis. We use two expert models, Seed-1.8 and DeepSeek-V3.2, to
evaluate the performance improvement of our method on the two
unsupervised tasks. For the same problem, the outputs of the two models
are simultaneously given to the expert models for an AB-test, where the
experts are required to determine which output is better.

The results show that both in self-personality understanding (a) and
self-emotion expression (b), the model at the later stage of training is
clearly better than the model at the early stage. This directly
demonstrates the effectiveness of our unsupervised method: by explicitly
optimizing the ERC task, the other two tasks can also be optimized in an
unsupervised manner. More analysis and observations on task entropy
reduction are provided in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Multi-task Training Metrics and Analysis ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
and specific examples can be found in Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Response Comparison Before and After Training ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression").

#### 4.4.2 Impact of Personality Traits on Reward Acquisition

To further analyze the influence of personality traits on obtaining
IOU-based prediction rewards, we select the five most frequent
personality categories from the clustering results for analysis. As
shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4.2 Impact of Personality Traits on Reward Acquisition ‣ 4.4 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
the column abbreviations correspond to the following traits: CPDE
denotes composed_practical_direct_efficient, EEIPRC denotes
emotional_expressiveness_interpersonal_playfulness_reactive_curiosity,
ERDCPD denotes
emotional_reactivity_defensive_confrontation_pragmatic_dominance, EDAE
denotes emotional_directness_assertive_engagement, and HRS denotes
humor_regulated_social.

|               |        |        |        |        |        |        |
|---------------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Model         | CPDE   | EEIPRC | ERDCPD | EDAE   | HRS    | AVG    |
| Seed-1.8      | 13.06% | 12.81% | 13.03% | 14.21% | 15.75% | 13.77% |
| DeepSeek-V3.2 | 10.25% | 10.89% | 9.64%  | 9.21%  | 10.21% | 10.04% |
| SELF-EMO-8B   | 57.09% | 58.83% | 58.16% | 56.32% | 61.98% | 58.48% |

Table 3: Distribution of personality traits predicted by different
models. SELF-EMO obtains significantly higher rewards across all
personality types.

By analyzing
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4.2 Impact of Personality Traits on Reward Acquisition ‣ 4.4 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
we observe that the optimized SELF-EMO achieves significantly higher
rewards than the two larger models. The calm and objective trait HRS
consistently yields higher rewards, while the more emotional and
confrontational ERDCPD results in lower rewards, indicating that
personality traits influence emotion recognition. More details on
training data composition are provided in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Data Analysis ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression").

## 5 Conclusion

In conclusion, we present SELF-EMO, a psychologically motivated
reinforcement learning framework that leverages three strongly
correlated tasks for collaborative entropy reduction. SELF-EMO achieves
state-of-the-art ERC performance under the Dataset-Unified Setting while
significantly reducing inference overhead, and the data produced during
training helps alleviate the scarcity of high-quality annotations in
this domain.

## Appendix B Data Analysis

We apply HDBSCAN to automatically cluster the extracted personality
descriptions. To avoid potential bias in the clustering process, the
original personality names are masked before clustering. In total, 74
clusters are obtained.

present the specific personality category names and their corresponding
counts.

It is worth noting that, due to the nature of the clustering algorithm,
some clusters may contain semantically similar descriptions.

## Appendix C Multi-task Training Metrics and Analysis

### C.1 Consistent Growth of Reward

As shown in
Fig. [5](#A3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ C.1 Consistent Growth of Reward ‣ Appendix C Multi-task Training Metrics and Analysis ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
under our experimental settings, SELF-EMO maintains a steady increase in
reward throughout training without experiencing collapse, across both
three public benchmarks (IEMOCAP, MELD, EmoryNLP) and the SELF-EMO split
test set.

Under different reward designs, compared to the reward curves on public
datasets based on accuracy
(Fig.[5(a)](#A3.F5.sf1 "In Figure 5 ‣ C.1 Consistent Growth of Reward ‣ Appendix C Multi-task Training Metrics and Analysis ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression")),
the IOU-based reward curve
(Fig.[5(b)](#A3.F5.sf2 "In Figure 5 ‣ C.1 Consistent Growth of Reward ‣ Appendix C Multi-task Training Metrics and Analysis ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"))
is smoother and more stable. This demonstrates that the proposed IOU
reward is not only more robust and generalizable, but also plays a key
role in stabilizing training.

![Refer to caption](2604.18003v1/picture/three_reward_plot.png)

(a) Acc of three emo benchmark.

![Refer to caption](2604.18003v1/picture/self_reward_plot.png)

(b) Self-emotion IOU reward

Figure 5: Steady Increase in Reward.

### C.2 Joint Entropy Reduction in Multi-task Learning

To further substantiate the effectiveness of the proposed multi-task
collaborative entropy reduction, we track the entropy of the policy
model throughout training. As shown in
Fig. [6(a)](#A3.F6.sf1 "In Figure 6 ‣ C.2 Joint Entropy Reduction in Multi-task Learning ‣ Appendix C Multi-task Training Metrics and Analysis ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
the entropy steadily decreases over time, with a notably sharper decline
in the early stages. This trend is consistent with
Fig. [5](#A3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ C.1 Consistent Growth of Reward ‣ Appendix C Multi-task Training Metrics and Analysis ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
where the reward improves most rapidly at the beginning of training,
highlighting the alignment between reinforcement learning dynamics and
entropy reduction.

In addition, we measure the entropy of the model on the two proposed
tasks: self-emotion generation $`T_{s}`$ and self-emotion expression
$`T_{e}`$ after each training epoch. Concretely, each checkpoint is
evaluated on the SELF-EMO test split, and the average token-level
entropy is computed for each task. As illustrated in
Fig. [6(b)](#A3.F6.sf2 "In Figure 6 ‣ C.2 Joint Entropy Reduction in Multi-task Learning ‣ Appendix C Multi-task Training Metrics and Analysis ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
both tasks exhibit a clear downward trend in entropy during training,
again with a more pronounced decrease in the early phase. This
consistent pattern across tasks supports the collaborative entropy
reduction hypothesis and suggests that supervised fine-tuning on the ERC
task effectively promotes performance gains in both self-emotion
generation and self-emotion expression.

![Refer to caption](2604.18003v1/picture/entropy_all_v2.png)

(a) Entropy dynamics of the policy model

![Refer to caption](2604.18003v1/picture/entropy_twotask.png)

(b) Entropy reduction in Self-Emotion tasks

Figure 6: Entropy reduction dynamics during multi-task training.

## Appendix D Response Comparison Before and After Training

As described in
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
we conduct our analysis using samples generated by the model at the
early stage of training and at the later stage of training. We then
adopt an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation framework to compare the performance
improvement of the model on the tasks of personality-conditioned
self-emotion generation and self-emotion expression. A concrete example
is shown in
Table [8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix D Response Comparison Before and After Training ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression").

In this task, the model is required to first perform reasoning in the
chain-of-thought process: (1) analyze the emotional state of the last
speaker in the conversation, (2) generate its own emotional state based
on the provided personality description and the current context, and (3)
produce a response that is consistent with both the contextual situation
and the specified personality, grounded in the analysis of others’
emotions and its own generated emotional state.

When applying the LLM-as-a-judge protocol, we instruct the expert model
Seed-1.8 to conduct the evaluation from five aspects: the personality
description, the contextual situation, the analysis of answer1, the
analysis of answer2, and the final comparison between answer1 and
answer2. During the evaluation process, we do not disclose any
additional information about the identities of answer1 and answer2,
ensuring that the expert model’s judgment is not influenced by the
source of the responses.

As shown in
Table [9](#A4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix D Response Comparison Before and After Training ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression"),
the expert model concludes that answer1 is the superior response under
the given personality and contextual constraints. In contrast, answer2
neither reflects the personality trait of a “casual, socially proactive
style” nor fits appropriately within the current conversational context.

To highlight the differences between the early and later stages of
training, we also provide additional examples as shown in
Table[10](#A4.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Appendix D Response Comparison Before and After Training ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression")
and
Table[11](#A4.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix D Response Comparison Before and After Training ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression").

## Appendix E Hyperparameter Configuration

We conduct all experiments using the VeRL training framework on a single
node equipped with 8 NVIDIA GPUs. The base model is either Qwen3-8B or
Qwen3-4B. Detailed hyperparameters are listed in
Table[12](#A5.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix E Hyperparameter Configuration ‣ SELF-EMO: Emotional Self-Evolution from Recognition to Consistent Expression").

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Hyperparameter | Value | Hyperparameter | Value |
| train_batch_size | 64 | rollout.n | 8 |
| max_prompt_length | 4096 | rollout.max_num_batched_tokens | 12400 |
| max_response_length | 8192 | rollout.gpu_memory_utilization | 0.5 |
| model.path | Qwen3-8B | rollout.tensor_model_parallel_size | 8 |
| actor.optim.lr | 1e-6 | ref.log_prob_micro_batch_size_per_gpu | 16 |
| actor.ppo_mini_batch_size | 32 | ref.fsdp_config.param_offload | True |
| actor.ppo_micro_batch_size_per_gpu | 16 | algorithm.use_kl_in_reward | False |
| actor.kl_loss_coef | 0.001 | trainer.critic_warmup | 0 |
| actor.kl_loss_type | low_var_kl | trainer.n_gpus_per_node | 8 |
| actor.entropy_coeff | 0 | trainer.nnodes | 1 |
| actor.fsdp_config.param_offload | False | trainer.save_freq | 480 |
| actor.fsdp_config.optimizer_offload | False | trainer.test_freq | 10 |
| rollout.log_prob_micro_batch_size_per_gpu | 16 | trainer.total_epochs | 3 |
````
